title: TPU flexible filament: what it is good for
excerpt: TPU bends and absorbs knocks. Here is when it is the right choice, and when a rigid material does the job better.
body: TPU is a flexible filament. A part printed in it bends, squeezes and springs back, which makes it the choice for phone cases, grips, gaskets and pads.
Protective covers and bumpers that should absorb a knock
Grips and handles that sit comfortably in the hand
A soft part does not hold its shape under load. For a bracket, a hinge or anything that must stay exactly the same size, use PLA+, PETG or nylon instead.
Print slowly. Fast moves make a flexible strand buckle in the feed path
Use a direct-drive extruder if your printer has one; it feeds TPU more reliably
Keep the part simple. Thin, tall, soft shapes wobble on the way up
Store the spool dry, like all filaments
Test one small part before printing a big order. A few millimetres of wall thickness changes how soft the finished piece feels.

title: Nylon (PA): strong parts for wear and load
excerpt: Nylon is tough and slightly flexible. It suits gears, clips and parts that rub, but it takes moisture from the air.
body: Nylon, also called PA, is one of the toughest common filaments. It resists wear, bends a little before it breaks, and handles repeated stress well.
Gears, hinges and clips that are used every day
Parts that rub against another part
Tools and holders that take a knock
Nylon absorbs water from the air. A wet spool prints with bubbles, rough surfaces and weak layers. Keep the spool sealed with desiccant, and dry it before printing if it has been open for a while.
Nylon also warps more than PLA. Use an enclosure if you can, and a build surface that holds it well, such as a textured plate with an adhesive.
Nylon is a good material for working parts. Expect slightly more effort to print it, and keep it dry.

title: PLA+ and tough PLA: when the upgrade is worth it
excerpt: Regular PLA is easy and sharp. PLA+ and tough PLA are a little stronger. Here is how to choose between them.
body: Standard PLA prints easily and gives crisp detail, but it is brittle. A part dropped on a hard floor can crack or snap. PLA+ and tough PLA are modified versions that bend a little more before they break.
Prototypes where looks matter more than strength
Parts that stay indoors and are not stressed
Choose PLA+ or tough PLA for
Brackets and clips that carry a little weight
Covers and cases that may be dropped
Parts that will be handled often
All PLA types soften at fairly low temperatures. A part left on a hot dashboard or in direct sun can deform. For heat, look at ASA, ABS or PETG.
The usual range for PLA printing is about 190 to 220 °C. Check the data sheet for the exact figure of the spool you buy.

title: Carbon-fibre filament: stiff, light, and matte
excerpt: Carbon-fibre filament makes stiff, light parts with a matte finish. It also wears down a standard nozzle, so you need the right hardware.
body: Carbon-fibre filament is a base plastic, usually PLA, PETG or nylon, mixed with short carbon fibres. The result is stiffer than the base material and has a dull, velvet-like surface.
Stiffer parts for their weight, such as drone parts and tool handles
A matte finish that hides fingerprints and small layer lines
Less warp than some unfilled materials
The fibres are hard and wear brass nozzles quickly. Use a hardened steel or ruby-tipped nozzle for carbon-filled material. A brass nozzle may last only a few spools.
Dry the spool before use, because the base plastic still absorbs moisture
Expect slightly more brittleness in thin sections; add wall thickness
Clean the nozzle often, since fibres can leave residue

title: Resin or filament: which one for fine detail
excerpt: Resin printers give very fine detail and a smooth surface. Filament printers are easier to run and cheaper per part. Here is how to choose.
body: Resin printers cure liquid resin with light, layer by layer. Filament printers melt plastic and lay it down as a thread. Both make 3D prints, but they suit different jobs.
Miniatures and figures with small faces, hands and text
Smooth, glossy surfaces with almost no layer lines
Functional parts that need strength or heat resistance
Lower running cost and simpler cleaning
Resin is more brittle than most filament. It needs washing in alcohol or a cleaner, then curing under UV light, and you must wear gloves because uncured resin irritates skin.

title: Wood-fill and silk filament: the finish you get
excerpt: Wood-fill and silk filaments look like real wood or shiny metal. They need slightly different settings to look their best.
body: Specialty filaments add a visible effect to a plain plastic. Wood-fill mixes in fine wood powder, so parts look like timber and can be sanded and stained. Silk filament has a glossy, satin look that catches the light.
Sand the part to show the wood grain, then stain or wax it
Use a larger nozzle, often 0.6 mm, to avoid clogs from the powder
Print slowly and keep the nozzle clean
Glossy colours show layer lines more than matte ones, so tune the layer height
Silk can be slightly less stiff than standard PLA; choose wall thickness with care
Test a small sample of each colour. Lighting changes how these finishes look a lot.

title: Translucent and glow filament for lamps
excerpt: Thin, translucent filament lets light through. Here is how to print a lamp shade that glows evenly.
body: Translucent and natural (unpainted) filament lets light pass through. A thin, single-wall lamp shade in a light colour glows warmly when a bulb sits inside it.
What makes a good lamp part
Thin walls, usually one or two perimeters, so light is not blocked
Even wall thickness, so the glow is even
A natural or white base colour, which glows more than dark colours
PLA and PETG are the usual choices. PETG is a little tougher and handles a warm bulb better. Keep the bulb small and the shade well ventilated.
Glow-in-the-dark filament stores light and fades over minutes. It does not light up by itself.

title: Filament storage: how moisture ruins a print
excerpt: Damp filament prints with bubbles, rough surfaces and weak parts. A few simple habits keep spools dry.
body: Most filaments absorb water from the air over time. Wet filament hisses and pops in the nozzle, and the printed part looks rough, stringy or weak. Nylon and PETG are the most sensitive, but PLA can be affected too.
Popping or crackling sounds while printing
Rough, bubbly surfaces and fuzzy top layers
Weak parts that snap along the layers
Keep spools in a sealed box with silica gel or a desiccant pack
Use a vacuum bag for long storage
Open only the spool you are printing
Re-dry the spool in a filament dryer or a low-temperature oven if the manufacturer allows it

title: Heat resistance: which material survives a hot place
excerpt: A part on a sunny sill or in a hot car can soften. Compare PLA, PETG, ASA and nylon to choose a material that stays put.
body: Heat changes how a 3D printed part behaves. Some materials begin to soften and sag at temperatures a car interior or a sunny window can reach.
PLA: softens at low temperatures. Good indoors, poor in a hot car
PETG: handles moderate heat better and is tough. A reasonable middle choice
ASA: designed for outdoor sun and heat, with good UV resistance
Nylon: handles heat well and is strong, but takes in moisture

For a part that will sit in the sun, choose ASA. For an indoor part that must not sag, PETG is a practical choice. Always check the data sheet for the heat deflection figure before you order a critical part.

title: How an FDM 3D printer works
excerpt: Most desktop 3D printers melt plastic and build it layer by layer. Here is what each part of the machine does.
body: Most home and studio printers use fused deposition modelling, often called FDM. Plastic filament is pulled into a hot nozzle, melted, and pushed out as a thread. The nozzle follows a path on each layer and the part grows upward one thin layer at a time.
Extruder: grips the filament and pushes it into the hot end
Hot end: heats the filament to melting point
Nozzle: the small opening where molten plastic comes out, often 0.4 mm
Build plate: the surface the part sticks to while it prints
Frame and motion system: moves the nozzle and the bed on accurate rails
Knowing these parts helps you find the cause of a problem. A poor first layer points to the bed. Weak parts can point to temperature or moisture. Most fixes start with one part of this list.

title: Bed levelling explained
excerpt: A level bed is the first step to a good print. Here is how levelling works, and how to check it without guesswork.
body: The nozzle must sit a very small distance above the build plate, roughly the thickness of a sheet of paper, at every point. If one corner is too high, the first layer does not stick there. If it is too low, the nozzle drags and scratches the plate.
Manual: turn the bed screws until a sheet of paper drags slightly at each corner and the centre
Automatic: a probe measures many points and corrects the first layer in software
Heat the bed to its normal temperature, since metal expands
Print a single-layer test square and look at the lines
Re-check after moving the printer or changing the build plate

title: Nozzle sizes: what changes when you switch
excerpt: The nozzle diameter sets the detail and speed of a print. Here is what 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6 mm nozzles each do well.
body: A nozzle is the opening the plastic leaves through. The most common size is 0.4 mm. Smaller and larger nozzles change the balance between detail and speed.
Finer lines and sharper small details
Slower printing, often several times longer
Clogs more easily with dirty filament
Faster printing for large, simple parts
Good for wood-fill and other filled filaments
When you change the nozzle, update the nozzle size in your slicer too, and check the first layer again. A mismatch between the slicer and the real nozzle is a common cause of poor prints.

title: Layer height: detail against speed
excerpt: Layer height is the thickness of each slice. Thin layers look smoother and take longer. Here is how to pick one.
body: Layer height is how thick each slice of the part is. A 0.2 mm layer is common for detailed work, and a 0.28 mm layer is used when speed matters more than smoothness.
Smoother surfaces with fainter layer lines
Better for curves and small detail
Faster prints, sometimes half the time
Good for functional parts where looks are secondary
Keep the layer height below about three quarters of the nozzle size. A 0.4 mm nozzle works well with layers between about 0.1 and 0.3 mm.

title: Enclosures: why they matter for ABS and ASA
excerpt: Materials that shrink as they cool need a warm, still space around the part. An enclosure gives that, and here is how.
body: ABS and ASA shrink as they cool. Without help, the corners of a large part lift off the bed and crack. A closed box around the printer keeps the air warm and still, so the part cools slowly and evenly.
Holds the air temperature steady around the part
Stops cold draughts from a fan or an open window
Keeps fumes from ABS and ASA contained
PLA, PETG and most TPU prints work without an enclosure. Keep the room away from fans and open windows, and print at a steady room temperature.
Ventilate the room when printing ABS or ASA, even with an enclosure. Keep the printer somewhere with airflow.

title: Build plate types: PEI, glass and textured
excerpt: The build plate decides whether a part sticks and then releases. PEI, glass and textured sheets each have their place.
body: The build plate is the surface the part is printed on. Good adhesion while printing and easy removal afterwards are both needed. No single plate does everything.
PEI sheet: sticks well to PLA, PETG and ABS once warm, and releases when cool
Smooth glass: gives a flat, glossy bottom surface; use an adhesive on some materials
Textured sheet: gives a matte finish on the bottom and grips well; good for PETG and nylon
Clean with isopropyl alcohol and no fingers on the surface
Replace a worn sheet before it starts to lift parts
Use a glue stick or adhesive only if the material needs it

title: Resin printer basics: curing, washing and safety
excerpt: A resin printer needs a wash and a cure after every print. Here is the routine that gives strong, clean results.
body: A resin printer cures liquid resin with UV light, layer by layer. The part that comes off the build plate is still soft and wet with resin. It needs two more steps before it is ready.
Print, then lift the build plate and let the excess resin drip off
Wash the part in isopropyl alcohol or a resin cleaner to remove the wet resin
Dry the part fully, then cure it under UV light for the time the resin data sheet gives
Wear nitrile gloves; uncured resin irritates skin
Work in a ventilated room and keep the resin away from food areas
Store resin in its bottle away from light and heat

title: Print speed and acceleration: fast without losing quality
excerpt: Faster printing saves time, but speed and acceleration can cause ringing and weak layers. Here is how to set them.
body: Print speed is how fast the nozzle moves when extruding. Acceleration is how quickly it reaches that speed. High values save time, but they make the frame shake and leave ripples on the surface.
Signs the speed is too high
Ringing: wavy lines near sharp corners
Missed steps or a head that shifts
Start from the slicer default for your material and printer
Raise the speed in steps of about 10 percent and print the same test part each time
Lower the acceleration first if ringing appears; it is often the cause
Outer walls look best when printed slower than the inner infill. Many slicers let you set them separately.

title: Stringing and oozing: how to stop the hairs
excerpt: Fine hairs between parts are stringing. They come from heat, retraction and moisture. Here is how to fix each cause.
body: Stringing is the thin hairs of plastic left between two parts of the print when the nozzle travels across an open gap. Oozing is the same thing, leaking out of the nozzle while it moves.
Temperature too high: lower it by 5 °C steps until the hairs stop
Retraction set too low: increase the retraction distance and speed a little
Wet filament: dry the spool, then print again
Travel speed too slow: raise the travel speed so the nozzle spends less time over gaps
A worn or dirty nozzle drips more. Clean it, and replace it if the tip is damaged.

title: Warping and lifting corners
excerpt: When the corners of a print lift off the bed, the plastic is shrinking unevenly. Here is what to change to keep it flat.
body: Warping happens when the bottom of a part cools and shrinks faster than the top. The corners lift and sometimes crack away from the plate. It is most common with ABS, ASA and large flat parts.
Heat the bed to the right temperature for the material
Use an enclosure to keep the air warm and still
Add a brim, a wide flat border around the part, so it holds to the bed better
Clean the build plate; oil from fingers stops adhesion
Turn off fans on the first few layers, if the slicer allows
Round the corners of a part, and avoid very large flat bases. A smaller footprint warps less.

title: Layer shifts and ringing: when the print moves
excerpt: A sudden shift in the layers or ripples across the surface point to the frame, the belts or the speed. Here is how to tell which.
body: A layer shift is a sudden sideways jump in the print, and every layer above it sits off-centre. Ringing is a set of ripples near sharp edges. They have different causes but often appear together.
Loose belts: tighten them until they hum a steady note when plucked, without being tight enough to bend the motor shaft
Loose pulleys or screws on the carriage
Print speed or acceleration too high for the frame
Tangled filament or a catch on the spool that stops the feed
High acceleration, so the frame vibrates at corners
A frame that is not rigid; check every bolt
A heavy print head or an unbalanced fan

title: Under-extrusion: gaps and weak walls
excerpt: When the printer does not push out enough plastic, walls come out thin and gappy. Here is how to find the cause.
body: Under-extrusion means the nozzle is not pushing out the planned amount of plastic. The walls look thin, there are gaps in the infill, and the part feels weak.
Nozzle blocked or partly clogged: clear it (see the clog article)
Filament too tight in the drive gear, or the gear is worn and slipping
Temperature too low for the filament, so it does not melt fully
Flow rate or extrusion multiplier set too low in the slicer
Wet filament that swells and resists the feed
Print a small cube. Measure the walls with calipers. If they are thin by a steady amount, adjust the flow multiplier in small steps.

title: First layer not sticking
excerpt: If the first layer does not stick, nothing above it will print well. Here is the order to check the bed, the nozzle and the settings.
body: The first layer is the foundation of the whole print. If it lifts, moves or leaves gaps, the print fails. Most first-layer problems come from the distance between nozzle and bed, or from a dirty surface.
Bed level: the nozzle is too high (gaps and ropes) or too low (scratches and blobs)
Build plate: clean it with isopropyl alcohol; apply a thin adhesive if the material needs it
Bed temperature: too cold means poor adhesion for PETG and ABS
First-layer speed: slow it down, often to about 20 to 30 mm/s
The filament itself. Wet filament and an old spool can change how the first layer lays down. Dry it and try again.

title: Nozzle clogs: how to clear them
excerpt: A clog stops the filament at the nozzle. Most can be cleared with heat, a cold pull or a fresh needle. Here is how.
body: A clogged nozzle prints thin lines, grinds the filament or does not extrude at all. The cause is usually dust, burnt filament or a piece of a previous colour stuck in the tip.
Heat the nozzle to the material temperature and push a little filament through by hand
Cold pull: heat the nozzle, push filament in, then cool to about 90 °C and pull the filament out quickly to take the debris with it
Use a fine cleaning needle while the nozzle is hot, and keep fingers clear
If the blockage is hard, remove the nozzle and soak or replace it
Clean the nozzle after changing colours or materials
Do not run the nozzle much below the printing temperature

title: Blobs and zits on the surface
excerpt: Small bumps and blobs on the outside of a print are a common sight. They come from retraction, seams and sometimes the slicer.
body: Blobs and zits are small bumps that appear on the surface, often in a line or in one spot. They happen when the nozzle pauses in one place long enough to leave a little extra plastic.
Seam placement: the start and end of each layer sit in the same place. Move the seam to a corner or a hidden side
Retraction too low, so plastic oozes while the nozzle moves
Temperature too high for the outer wall
Slow outer walls with long pauses
Set the seam to hidden corners, tune retraction in small steps, and lower the temperature a little. Print a test cube and compare.

title: Supports that will not come off
excerpt: Supports should snap away cleanly. When they fuse to the part, the settings are usually too dense or too close. Here is how to fix that.
body: Supports hold up overhangs while the part prints. They should break away cleanly. When they fuse to the surface, the part is left with scars and rough patches.
Too dense: a high support density bonds more strongly to the part
Interface layers set too close to the part; add a small gap, usually one layer
Temperature too high, which makes the plastic stick harder
Support material the same as the model material, which bonds together
Lower the support density and use a simple pattern
Use a support interface layer with a small gap
Design overhangs at 45 degrees or less so supports are rarely needed
Consider tree supports, which touch the part at fewer points
